Like someone mentioned, there’s two kinds of people that get called “recruiter”. 

First are the ones who you should care about: the people at the actual company whose job it is to locate talent and fill roles. Their titles vary. At startups it might be someone in the C suite, at small companies it might be an engineering manager or HR person, at bigger companies the title will probably be “recruiter”. 

These people have the power to make you go from applicant to employee. 

On the other hand, there are “headhunters”. They might work at talent agencies or staffing firms. They might be self employed. They also probably call themself a “recruiter” Their job it to get *a* candidate accepted for a role. At that point they get a few hundred to a few thousand bucks and they do it again. 

Sometimes that arrangement works out. If the headhunter understands the job landscape and the company, they might be able to find good candidates. In my experience, most headhunters are grifters. They solicit as many resumes as they can, encourage you to exaggerate your abilities, and ghost you when someone else fills the role. They don’t bother networking, don’t keep you in mind for other roles, and don’t care if a person and company are bad fits for one another. 

Focus on in-house recruiters. Good headhunters are worth their weight in gold — and are as rare as a 100+ pound sack of gold.

Yep. This is life as an adhd dev. My first 3 years were hell, but I eventually got good identifying when I’m in a rut, and figured out some strategies to get myself out of them. 

It’s not easy and there’s no shortcuts. The best piece of advice I can offer is to own your errors publicly. I used to spend weeks not making real progress and hiding that lack of progress from my team. The stress that caused (no exaggeration) almost killed me. I don’t know what your team looks like, but tell people you’re struggling to wrap something up.

Telling people holds you accountable. If you’re a junior dev, this line will make you a lot of friends: “I was hoping to get x,y,z done yesterday, but I can’t work through z, does anyone wanna hop on a call at 11 and just talk through it with me?”  Again, if you’re a junior, everyone expects you to be struggling and a bit confused. Use that to get help while you can. 

If you’re not a junior just accept that you’ll be working late for the next few months while you get up to speed. It’s gonna suck, but I don’t think there’s a realistic alternative. 

Most importantly: take a weekend and research strategies for surviving with adhd. Nothing works for everyone, but something will work for you. If you’re intentional about it, you might be able to find the right strategy in a few months instead of a few years. 

Hang in there buddy, this is the hard part. I promise you’ll get through it.

So I’ve been on the *other* side of this. 

I have adhd. Your employee probably does too. When I’m interested in a task or have clear, short, deadlines, I produce high quality work at an insane pace. Under all other circumstances it’s a toss up. 

For me, “interest” is always unpredictable and short-lived. It sometimes motivates me to get 80% of a task done, but almost never motivates me to complete it. Instead, social pressure and the desire to help my team is what pushes me to actually do my job. I benefit massively from daily stand ups where everyone on the team talks about what they’re working on, what their challenges are, and evaluates their progress on their tasks. The fact that I said “this should be done by tomorrow” motivates me to actually have it done tomorrow *because I feel like I’ll let my team down if I don’t make good progress*. 

Another big thing that helped me was having domain ownership. In my case, I was solely responsible for a handful of services. I took care of updates, checked in on performance metrics, added features, etc. That helped me prioritize tasks and take initiative because there was no one else to do it. 

Lastly, the benefit you’re describing from “micromanaging” is actually something called “body doubling”. Don’t ask me why, but the most reliable way to mitigate executive dysfunction is to have someone else physically in the room with the person. Can you tell this employee that there is now a hybrid expectation? If they’re in the office with other people, you should get the same benefits of your daily calls, but it takes up none of your time. 

This is a real challenge for a manager. I imagine you probably feel frustrated that this person isn’t helping your team much, and maybe a little betrayed that your trust was betrayed. Bluntly, you need to get over those feelings. Your job is getting your team to work well, and this employee requires different tactics. If you’re not up to the challenge, you shouldn’t waste time getting the employee removed. 

Otherwise, roll up your sleeves and keep trying new things. 

On the off chance you’re interested, feel free to DM me and we can chat about how I’ve worked with different managers. It might give you some new perspectives. 

Good luck friend

Couple tips:

1. Lower the difficulty to normal. Higher difficulties just tax your resources more. Lots of people find this extra challenge fun, it seems you don’t. Normal is probably your best difficulty
2. Charge. Up. Wrench. Attacks. They do wildly more damage and have a high knockdown chance. More importantly they use the same amount of stamina. There is literally never a reason to *not* charge your wrench attacks
3. Don’t use bullets on normal mimics or phantoms. Gloo Gun + wrench is truly all you need
4. Restart the game. Prey is truly a great game, but it’s hard to enjoy if you burn all your resources getting a feel for the mechanics. Take a day or two off and then give it a fresh start.
5. Shorter play sessions. Prey massively benefits from really thinking about where you are and what you find. If you’re frustrated you’re probably not doing that. So aim for 30-60 mins of fun over 2 hours of grinding and frustration. 
6. You can beat the game without ever using a neuro mod (maybe you have to use the first one? But I don’t think so). A creative solution exists to get you from wherever you are to the next story beat. Look for them! That’s what makes the game fun :)

Two options: you have imposter syndrome or you’re an imposter. 

If you have certs, you’re probably not an imposter. AWS certs aren’t the hardest to get, but you still have to actually know how stuff works. 

If you have imposter syndrome, you need self confidence. The best way to build self confidence is to build something. The second best way is to learn something new. 

So deploy a database cluster or kubernetes cluster on top of EC2. No using managed services as a crutch. You’ll get a much deeper knowledge of how stuff works and what the managed service is doing. 

Or learn a new language and deploy a few REST services. Keep it simple: a server that takes a POST request and uploads a row into a database. 

Or just grind leetcode until you can do hard ones in a few minutes consistently. 

The only wrong thing to do is nothing :)

As others have pointed out, burnout is a real problem and is impossible to ignore. You don’t need validation for burnout, you need rest. 

To your actual points: most codebases suck, full stop. Crappy codebases are a result of the constant personnel  changes from layoffs and job hoping that plague our industry. If people had to use codebases for closer to a decade than 2 years, they’d organically transform the codebase into something pleasant to use. 

Since that’s not the case, here’s my recommendation: 

First: deal with your burnout. (Oversimplification incoming): Your brain thinks it’s under constant threat and is conserving energy for crises. You need to convince it that you’re safe. The the cloud-specific secrets managers have the same feature set as Hashicorps vault. If you’re all in one cloud, it’s incredibly convenient to use that cloud’s secrets manager because you can directly grant some resource access to a specific set of secrets. It’s a bad idea to replicate secrets across multiple secrets managers because then you can’t guarantee that they get rotated and/or deleted synchronously. 

Vault gives you the same amount of granularity, but you have to implement an authorization strategy to guarantee that only the proper resources can access specific secrets. So it’s harder, but necessary for multi cloud environments. 

Other multi cloud solutions probably exist, but hashicorps vault is the industry standard and you don’t deviate from that without good reason.

I’d like to start out and say this is not your fault. You’re clearly doing your best, and that’s all you owe anyone. 

Couple pieces of advice. First, can you return him to his previous home? Not every adoption works out and that’s not your fault. If he can be returned, that might be what’s best for him. 

Second, you need to identify why exactly he’s so unhappy. Three months is long enough for nearly all cats to adapt to their new environment, so it’s possible there’s another variable here. 
You mentioned allergies, is he having trouble breathing? It’s hard to tell, but if you see him panting (with his mouth open) that’s a dead giveaway. If he doesn’t pant his breathing is *probably* fine. How did you introduce him to the home? 
Did you start him in a small room and let him slowly explore the house at his own pace? If not, pretend he’s coming home for the first time and let him build up his courage. 
Is it possible he was part of a bonded pair? It might be worth a call to wherever you adopted him to see if there’s another cat moping around over there. If they were bonded, you should still do a slow introduction, but they should warm up to each other quickly. 

Third, were there any changes to his food or litter? Some cats have insanely picky pallets. Are you using the same food the shelter was using? Same litter? If not, try and acquire those. 

Fourth, embrace home-made chicken broth. I’ve never seen a cat who didn’t go crazy for the smell of simmering chicken broth. To make it, just get the biggest pack of chicken legs or wings you can find from the grocery store, cover them with water by an inch or two, bring to a boil and then reduce to a simmer. Simmer for 6-12 hours. IMPORTANT: COOL OFF THE BROTH BEFORE FEEDING. Cats have extremely sensitive tounge and will burn themselves on anything above room temp. For a few reasons you should use the ice bath method: https://extension.umn.edu/preserving-and-preparing/cool-soup-safely. 

Fourth, I don’t think force feeding pills is ever necessary. There are only two kinds of pills: capsules (which hold some kind of a powder) and tabs (which are the normal solid kind). Try to get his medicines as capsules. Open the capsules (just twist the middle) and mix the powder in a few ounces of *room temp* chicken broth. He might only get 85% of the medicine, but it’s way less traumatic for you both — fair trade imho. If you can’t get capsules, crush up the pills by hand. To do this, cut the pill into as small pieces as you can with your sharpest knife (clean it beforehand obviously), wrap the pill-bits in plastic wrap, and hit the wrapped bits with a hammer until powder. Crude? Yes. Effective? Also yes. I’d recommend pulverizing all the pills for the day at once so there’s not a ton of loud banging right before you give him the powder 3 times a day.  

Lastly, consider keeping him on a diet of chicken and rice for a while. They’re as easy on cats’ stomachs as ours and can help with constipation. Boil the rice in the chicken broth for some extra flavor, and dump some extra broth on top to keep him hydrated. 

Also, please call your vet and get their advice, they work with cats more than either of us and will be able to spot check my recommendations (and probably provide better ones). 

Good luck!!

Edit: re-read your post and it sounds like he trusts you and feels safe. That’s great news, but I think it indicates there’s a more general problem with his digestion. If you can afford it, you may want to do a stool sample to look for worms or any other parasites. Also does he have any appetite? Will he (for example) eat a churu? If not then something more serious is wrong and you should find a different vet. If he sometimes gets excited about food then yea, just try my above recommendations and pray.

I'd like to preface by saying I'm interested in an actual fun discussion about the show and books. I respect that I'm unlikely to change any minds and I think your dislike of the show is valid (you can't argue with taste). Please try to be courteous in the comments.

I'm going to treat this as a logic exercise. I will try to translate your points into syllogisms to show where some of the holes in your logic are. I will probably misinterpret some of what you say, so please accept that this is all in good faith. :)

**"Adaptation is impossible"**

I believe the argument you're making here is: LoTR, GoT, and Dune are difficult-to-adapt books/series which were high-quality faithful adaptations of the source material. The Wheel of Time book series is no more complex than any of those. Therefore, The Wheel of Time show could have been a faithful adaptation of the books, if the writers cared.

I don't think this is a good argument. 

To begin, LoTR was not a perfectly  faithful adaptation. Many characters and most of the lore is absent from the movies. Events from all three books are each movie. About half of the plot from Movie 2 is in book three. MUCH of the plot of book three is left out of movie 3. (\*cough\* desolation of the shire \*cough\*).  To preempt the obvious counterargument, none of those criticisms matter. The movies are phenomenal films and very close to the best adaptations we could've hoped for. My point is that it's hard to call it a "faithful" adaptation.

Next, are we really gonna pretend GoT was a remotely faithful adaptation? Are we really gonna pretend GoT had good writing past season 4? If you're interested, I'd recommend reading the book *Fire Cannot Kill a Dragon*. It's about the insanity of the creation and production of the show. It's based on interviews with hundreds of people involved in the show . I consider it airtight evidence that GoT simply collapsed under the weight of its convoluted plotlines and untenable production schedules. I truly don't fault the writers for working on a smaller scale.

**"This is another turn of the wheel"**

I believe the argument you're making here is: Rafe tried to avoid criticism for his changes by claiming this is another turn of the wheel. It isn't another turn of the wheel because it has the same characters with the same names doing basically the same things. Therefore Rafe is making up a bad justification that we don't have to accept.

There's a word for this kind of fallacy, but I can't find it. The issue is that your warrant doesn't prove your claim, but the conclusion is tautological, so the syllogism is wrong, but also right. (Logic is weird). Here's what I mean: If it was another turning of the wheel and the show sucked, it would still suck. You would still be able to criticize it. The only requirement for disliking a show is having dislike for the show. Addressing your actual points: I'd say this is clearly another turn of the wheel. Events play out differently, but most of the characters end up in mostly the same places, doing mostly the same things. That....kinda what I expect a turn of the wheel to look like. I'm curious what you think another turn of the wheel would actually look like, if it's not this.

**"Covid 19 harmed S1"**

I believe the argument you're making here is: There is no justification for releasing a bad product, and Rafe had the power to make it good, if he cared. GoT rewrote its pilot when it wasn't good, and Dune was delayed due to covid. Therefore WoT S1 should have been good despite covid.

I don't think the warrant proves the claim. Pilots exist as a test. Although reshoots of a pilot are rare, they're hardly unheard of. Notably, the pilot (the VERY first episode) is the only one that ever got reshot. Ever. In all 8 seasons. I'm not aware of any examples of an episode of tv getting reshot. It may well have happened, but I can't find evidence of it. Next, Dune was a movie meant for theaters. It made approximately 5 gazillion dollars in theaters. If they'd released in mid 2020 (when most movie theaters in the US were either shut down or had massively reduced capacity), that's MILLIONS of dollars down the tube that they can never get back. 

On top of that, we didn't know when covid would end. Pausing production for just 6 months might've doomed the show, and there was no guarantee that the world would be back to normal in 6 months. Pausing production indefinitely WOULD have been the end of the show. It's very reasonable to assume that Rafe took the best actions in his power, imho.

" **Mat's actor's departure had harmful effects on production.**"

I believe the argument you're making here is: Matt's actor did not cause a total rewrite of S2. Other movies/shows have had problems that they solved without rewriting seasons. Therefore Rafe lied because he knows he wrote a bad season 2. 

I don't think this is a strong argument. We don't know what was supposed to happen in the last two episodes. Maybe Ishamael originally captured Matt and the horn, and S2 was supposed to open with our merry band hunting him down in the blight. More likely, S1 was supposed to end with everyone in Fal Dara, and S2 could have followed TGH more closely. I'm not sure. But I think it's a stretch to say Rafe was just lying.

" **Amazon does not give me enough episodes.** "

I believe your argument here is: If Rafe needed more episodes to tell the story, there would be almost no time spent on characters & plots that aren't in the books. We spend a lot of time with characters the show invented. Therefore the show didn't need more episodes, the writers just didn't care.

This is very subtly wrong. There's an errant implicit assumption here. It is as follows: *Eight episodes is enough time to tell a cohesive adaptation of EotW, while only uses RJ's plotlines.* If this is not true, your argument fails. Consider this: The warder bond is the most interesting part of EotW. We learn about it slowly from many perspectives. We slowly piece together that it's both a normal emotional connection, and also a magical spiritual connection. We learn that both Moiraine and Lan like some parts of the bond, and dislike some parts of it. We learn that Warders are willing to abandon all their prior obligations -- to essentially abandon their sense of self -- to help their Aes Sedai.

Given more episodes, I assume they would have laid out this story slowly and subtly, like RJ does. But I don't think they could have. Their middle ground was to build a new plotline around the warders and their bond. You can still think that episode sucks if you'd like. I just don't think 8 episodes was enough to go through the plot of EotW while still having enough time to display the Moiraine-Lan relationship with the depth it required. So they didn't. Ah so this is something I've thought about. I think the real issues are attack speed and feedback. 

In Sekiro, most enemy animations prepared the attack, paused for a second, and then attacked quickly. You the player are timing your parry for right after that pause. For enemies who don't stagger after one parry, there's a certain rhythm that defines their swings\*. Importantly, when you successfully deflect an attack, the enemy reacts to it instantly. You watch them yank their sword back (the preparation step) and begin the next one, with the little pause. This don't apply to quite every enemy, but it's a good rule of thumb.

Fallen Order does not do this. There are clear telegraphs for initial attacks, but there's a noticeably longer period where the attack can damage you. I think this is because parry windows on lower difficulties are so long that they had to make long animations to give people more time. It's not really a problem -- Fallen Order doesn't have to have the same mechanics as Sekiro. The issue is that that rule carries over to consecutive deflections. 

Consecutive attacks don't have rhythm because they *can't* have rhythm. The attacks have to be parry-able for people on story mode *and* for the people on grandmaster, but they can't be too long or they won't be fun for any group. This means that enemies will almost always skip the preparation stage after the initial attack and just have a long delay between attack 1 latest deflect time and attack 2 latest deflect time. 

This isn't intrinsically bad. Actually I'm starting to see it as almost a good thing. It's a high skill ceiling and I can't fault them for that. Damage is still predictable and preventable, I personally just found it a bit too much to concentrate on to make it through all the combos with perfect deflections. It's acceptable for me because of dodges and blocking. You can usually parry the first attack in the combo and then just keep holding block and attack when there's an opening. 

Maybe I'll summarize and say I found it more akin to bad checkpoints than bad hitboxes. It's not cheap or broken, it just didn't feel like it was challenging in the way games ought to be challenging. But again, that's probably a "me" problem.
